title: CDN & Edge Caching
summary: CDNs move content physically closer to users. Learn how edge servers cache content, how requests find the nearest one, and when the cache goes stale.

blocks.markdown:
A **CDN (Content Delivery Network)** is a globally distributed set of **edge servers** that store copies of your content close to users.

- Without a CDN every request travels to your **origin server** — slow for distant users.
- With a CDN a nearby **edge** answers the request in milliseconds instead of hundreds.
- CDNs also absorb traffic spikes so your origin isn't crushed.
- Related: [network-performance-qos](network-performance-qos), [dns](dns).

blocks.subTitle: Why it matters
blocks.markdown:
Two concrete gains from a CDN.

| Benefit | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Lower latency | Edge is physically closer to the user |
| Less origin load | Edge serves cached replies; origin sleeps |

A user in Mumbai hitting a US origin may wait 200 ms. The same request to a Mumbai edge takes ~5 ms.

**Origin** is your own server — the authoritative source for all content.

**Edge** (also called a **PoP, Point of Presence**) is a CDN node in a data centre near users. It caches a copy of content it has already fetched.

- Origin is the source of truth; edges are read-through caches in front of it.
- The CDN may have hundreds of PoPs worldwide.

blocks.sectionTitle: How content gets to the edge
blocks.subTitle: Pull vs push
blocks.markdown:
Two strategies for getting content onto edge servers.

- **Pull CDN** — edge fetches from origin on the first cache miss, then caches the result. Simple; content is only pulled when requested. Most CDNs (Cloudflare, Fastly) default to pull.
- **Push CDN** — you proactively upload content to every PoP. Good for large files (video) where you know demand will be high immediately. Requires managing uploads.

Pull is the default; push trades upload overhead for zero first-miss penalty.

When a request arrives at an edge:

- **Cache hit** — edge has a fresh copy → serves it immediately, origin never contacted.
- **Cache miss** — edge has no copy (or copy is stale) → fetches from origin, caches it, returns it.

**TTL (Time To Live)** is how long the edge keeps a cached copy before treating it as stale. Set via `Cache-Control: max-age=<seconds>` on the origin response.

High TTL = fewer misses but stale content risk. Low TTL = fresher but more origin hits.

**Cache invalidation** is telling edges to discard a cached copy before its TTL expires.

- **Purge** — CDN API call that removes specific URLs from all PoPs immediately.
- **Versioned URLs** — embed a content hash in the filename (`main.a3f9.js`). New deploy → new URL → old entry just expires naturally.
- **Surrogate keys / cache tags** — tag groups of objects (e.g. `product-42`) and purge the whole group at once.

Versioned URLs are the simplest reliable approach for static assets.

blocks.subTitle: Pitfall: stale after deploy
blocks.markdown:
Common mistake: deploy a new HTML file but forget to purge the old CDN cache.

- Users get old HTML referencing new JS filenames → broken app.
- Fix: **always purge or version** HTML on each deploy. HTML TTL should be short (60 s) even if asset TTLs are long (1 year with versioned URLs).

blocks.sectionTitle: How requests reach the nearest edge
blocks.subTitle: Anycast
blocks.markdown:
**Anycast** is a routing technique where many edge servers share the same IP address. The internet routes a packet to whichever server is closest by BGP metric.

- No DNS lookup per region — one IP, internet routing does the geography.
- Used by Cloudflare, Fastly for their edge networks.
- Contrast **unicast**: one IP = one host. Anycast: one IP = closest of many.

Benefit: zero config failover — if a PoP goes down, traffic auto-routes to the next nearest.

blocks.sectionTitle: How requests reach the nearest edge
blocks.subTitle: DNS-based routing
blocks.markdown:
Older CDNs use **DNS-based routing** instead of anycast.

- CDN's authoritative DNS detects user's resolver location and returns the IP of the nearest PoP.
- Works at DNS resolution time — every region gets a different A record.

Downside: DNS TTL adds latency to failover (must wait for caches to expire). Anycast fails over in seconds; DNS-based can take minutes. See [dns](dns).

blocks.subTitle: Static vs dynamic
blocks.markdown:
Not all content belongs on a CDN edge.

- **Cache aggressively** — images, CSS, JS bundles, fonts, video. Same bytes for every user; long TTL safe.
- **Cache carefully** — public API responses with short TTL (product listings). Saves origin but risks brief staleness.
- **Don't cache** — user-specific pages (dashboards, carts), auth tokens, POST/PUT responses, real-time data.

Key test: *would every user in this region get the same bytes?* If yes, cache it.

blocks.subTitle: Cache-Control header
blocks.markdown:
Origin controls CDN behavior via HTTP headers.

- `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable` — cache for 1 year; never revalidate (use on versioned assets).
- `Cache-Control: no-store` — never cache, ever.
- `Cache-Control: s-maxage=60` — shared (CDN) cache TTL 60 s; browser may differ.
- `Surrogate-Control` / `CDN-Cache-Control` — some CDNs strip `Cache-Control` before forwarding to the browser; use these for CDN-only TTL.

blocks.subTitle: What is a CDN and why use one?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a CDN and why would you use one?**

A CDN is a network of edge servers spread globally that cache copies of your content near users. Use one to reduce latency (edge is closer than origin), cut origin bandwidth costs, absorb traffic spikes, and improve availability under DDoS.

blocks.subTitle: How does anycast route requests?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How does a request reach the nearest CDN edge using anycast?**

All PoPs advertise the same IP via BGP. Routers naturally forward packets to the topologically closest PoP — no DNS lookup, no application logic. If a PoP fails, BGP withdraws its route and traffic shifts to the next closest in seconds.

blocks.subTitle: Pull vs push CDN; cache invalidation; what not to cache
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Pull vs push CDN — when does each fit?**

Pull: edge fetches on first miss; zero setup, good for unpredictable traffic. Push: you pre-upload to all PoPs; good for large files with predictable high demand (live video).

**Q: How do you invalidate cached content immediately?**

Purge via CDN API for targeted URLs, use cache tags to purge groups, or — best — use versioned URLs (hash in filename) so deploys never need purge.

**Q: What should you never cache on a CDN?**

User-specific data (shopping carts, dashboards), session tokens, POST/PUT responses, anything with real-time accuracy requirements. Cache only content that is the same for all users.
